questions.q: According to this lesson, what is the real measure of CRM success?
options: The total number of software licenses purchased
Whether the numbers coming out of the system are trustworthy and actionable, not just that the software was adopted
How many employees log in at least once a month
How visually appealing the CRM's dashboards look
questions.explain: Buying licenses isn't the goal — the data inside has to be reliable enough that leadership can actually act on the numbers it produces.

questions.q: Which metric is described as what sales is judged on, alongside win rate and deal size?
options: Case volume
Cost per lead
Customer satisfaction (CSAT)
Pipeline — the total value of open opportunities
questions.explain: Pipeline is the forward-looking measure of expected revenue, built from tracked opportunities — one of sales' core metrics.

options: The share of leads that convert into opportunities
The average time it takes to close a support case
The share of customers who leave or don't renew
The total ad spend per lead generated
questions.explain: Churn rate is a service/retention metric — the proportion of customers who leave rather than stay.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a high lead volume with a terrible conversion rate is usually a marketing problem, not a sales problem?
options: Because sales teams are never responsible for conversion rate
Because lead volume and conversion rate are unrelated metrics
Because marketing has no influence over who becomes a lead
Because it usually means marketing is attracting the wrong people, not that sales is failing to close them
questions.explain: The lesson states that lots of leads with a poor conversion rate points to marketing drawing in the wrong audience.

questions.q: What does this lesson say happens to win rate and pipeline when opportunities are left sitting in a stale stage?
options: They automatically recalculate correctly regardless of stale data
Win rate improves while pipeline stays accurate
Both numbers become meaningless, since they rely on opportunities being kept current
Stale opportunities are automatically excluded with no effect on the numbers
questions.explain: Every metric depends on good underlying data — stale opportunity stages directly undermine both win rate and pipeline calculations.
